translation:
In summer they saw much rasayan (a miracle-abundance) in the field, and among it there would also have been watermelons; Maharaj Jivanji must have welcomed the saint-devotees with these watermelons. There is another legend that at Aritha, Maharaj Jivanji made a field of vaal-papdi (a green bean) turn lush and green; that field is at the edge of the village, and nowadays, because of the polluted atmosphere, the devotees' minds are drawn toward worldly amusements rather than toward it, so it is known by the name "the field of vaal-papdi," and it is regrettable that the devotees have built a Shiv temple there. There is yet another confusion: whether Maharaj Jivanji showed Haribhai this great rasayan at Shahapura or at Aritha -- this question arises, but if we think it over sensibly, it can be said that seeing the way Maharaj Jivanji used to carry on the business of farming at Shahapura, Haribhai too must have been inspired to farm in the same way; so whatever vaal-papdi and other greens he grew in his own field, he must have given it the name "Maharaj Jivanji made the field of vaal-papdi turn green," expressing his gratitude to Maharaj Jivanji in that way. Whichever of these is true, one thing is certain: Maharaj Jivanji used to farm, and he must have inspired the devotees to live by earning through their own labor. To become self-reliant is Maharaj Jivanji's principle.

**KARMA PANJAR -- The Cage of Karma**

_Nar tatha ghodana kalbut rachi kripanathe atmane bandaginu puchhu te_ (Having fashioned the molds -- kalbut -- of man and horse, the Merciful Lord asked the soul about devotion.)

Compared to a devotee, it takes the Merciful Lord ten to twenty days. God did not fashion sensory pleasures (bhog) for those of tamasic (dull, dark) disposition, but this universe imagines that all pleasures were made for its own sake; in truth, the Merciful Lord made all pleasures for the sake of His saints. On the day the Merciful Lord created creation, He arranged and built the universe in just such a fitting way, and set it going.

The Vaishnav Jivandasji said: at one time, the Merciful Lord fashioned the kalbut (the wooden foot-shaped mold that is hammered inside a shoe) of a number of souls -- that is, so that the tamasic disposition of His own creation might not manifest within their own pure form, He fashioned these molds out of that tamasic tendency. Among them He made some into horses and made some souls into men.

Then the Merciful Lord first asked the men: "Will you do devotion, worship, and hymn-singing, or will you take on riding -- that is, enjoy sensory pleasures?" Some said, "We will do devotion, worship, and hymn-singing." And some others said, "We will take riding" (that is, enjoy pleasures). Those who agreed to take riding He made into horses; and those who had earlier been made horses He now made into men. Then the Merciful Lord spoke to those He had made men, asking: "Will you do remembrance, worship, and devotion, or will you take riding" (that is, become sadhus, mendicants, renunciants who sit and are fed)? Of these, a few said, "We will do remembrance and worship," and half said, "We will take riding" (become sadhus, renunciants, and so on). Then those who had agreed to devotion and worship became householders -- men and women living in the world -- and those who had agreed to riding (sadhus, mendicants, renunciants, yogis, ritualists) were made into horses. He made them the burden-bearers of sadhana, meditation, concentration, tantra, mantra, ritual, pilgrimage, vows, and so on.

A kalbut is the wooden mold, shaped like a foot, that cobblers make in order to fashion shoes; they wrap leather around this mold and make the shoe. This wooden mold is called a kalbut. In order to create the universe for souls, God made 8.4 million kinds of kalbut-molds for the 8.4 million species (yonis), and He filled souls into bodies of that shape; and so, whatever action the souls dwelling in that cage made of a body perform is called karma panjar, the cage of karma. Adhyaruji has spoken of the "victory cage" (vije pinjar).

_Harini sharanagat vije pinjar dayanidhi, riddhi akshaypad dataro._ (Sharanagati -- surrender: for the soul that lives in surrender to God, the cage that is its body is a victory cage, O treasury of mercy -- and it grants that soul a happiness greater even than riches and supernatural powers, riddhi-siddhi.)

Kabirji has called the soul like a parrot in a cage, and gives it this counsel.

**(Mangal Aarti)**

_Ram kaho panjarke suva, Ram kaho re panjarke suva.
Haju lagi khabar padat nahi andha, dhandho karat sakal jag muva. (Tek)
Ghadi re sutare kahero kino, haju lagi saaj nishchal nahi huva.
Anta kaal ripu hot manjari, haari chalyo jaise juvari juva. (Ram)
Asha met paanch panihari, khutat naahi karam la karva.
Kahe Kabir jene hari ras chakhyo, vaahike mukh amritras chuva. (Ram)_

O soul, like a parrot shut up in the cage of the body, chant and remember Ram. O unwitting, blind soul, you still have not understood that all the world dies away doing worldly deeds. God the carpenter has hollowed out the trunk of the human body -- like a palm or date-palm tree -- that is, He has fashioned it into a boat; but you, sitting in that boat, have not yet decided what provisions of devotion and worship you will carry along with you. So, at the final hour, it is like gamblers who play dice by balancing a lamp on a cat's head as a wager -- at the very moment of the decisive win, the cat, seeing a mouse, leaps, the lamp falls, and so the gambler loses. As that cat becomes the gambler's enemy, so too will you, like that gambler, lose the game that is human birth, and go to Yama's abode. In this world, giving up cravings, one draws out through the five senses -- like women drawing water -- the water of sensory pleasure from the well that is worldly existence; yet the water that is the bondage of karma never runs out. But Kabirji says: those who have tasted the flavor of devotion to Hari have had the good fortune of drinking, from their own mouths, the ambrosial flavor of supreme happiness.

Revered Yadunath has written, in Lintiyu no. 105, page 11: "Only when the cage becomes victorious does one come to chant Ram." The body indeed came to be prepared through the working of destiny (prarabdha), but you have not yet decided what to do with this human body. The soul is shut up in the cage that is the body; if it is not protected, the cat that is time (kaal) will devour it.

Karma is of two kinds: enjoined (vihit) karma and forbidden (nishiddh) karma. The kinds of enjoined karma are: nitya (daily, obligatory), naimittik (occasional), kamya (desire-driven), and prayashchit (expiatory). Those who follow the path of karma analyze karma in this way, but we ourselves are entirely untouched by karma. Maharaj Adhyaruji, too, says that devotees are not bound by karma.

_Abhakta janpe karma karave, karma bhogvava deh dharave, sevak karma kashano? Hari Hari. ||8||_ (You, O God, make non-devotees perform actions, and make them take on a body in order to reap the fruits of those actions; but for Your servant, what karma can there be?)

_Atmape tu karma karave, karma bhogvava deh dhaveraro, pamya sharan Hari Parbrahm Rai. ||7||_ (You make the soul perform actions and make it take on a body to reap the fruits of karma; but I have found refuge in You, O Hari Parbrahm, the King.)

Thus Adhyaruji has shown these words twice. Further, regarding the devotee and the non-devotee, Adhyaruji says:

_Sevak janne dayal tu, kaal tu bhagat vihin. ||4||_ (To the devotee You are merciful, but to one without devotion You are death itself, kaal.)

Thakkar, in his book on the doctrine of karma, has tried to prove that we must take birth according to our karma. But for those of us who are devoted to God, even though we perform actions, karma does not touch us. This principle holds both spiritually and, by ordinary worldly conduct, in that a master is held responsible for the wrongdoing of his servant. The law, too, follows this very same rule; hence it is known by the name of the master's liability for the servant's wrongdoing. Nor is there anything wrong in that -- it holds in divine law as well. On this basis Adhyaruji argues, on the strength of this legal principle, that for the servant, what karma can there be? Your servant performs actions only in Your service, so You alone are responsible for his actions. Indeed Adhyaruji states:

_Heli re nirbhay tuhaj ek, kijtan karma laage nahi e. ||25||_ (O Lord, You alone are wholly without fear of any kind, and so whatever act You perform, You are never bound by the karma of doing it.)

By this same principle, since the devotee and God are held to be one, whatever the devotee does, he does with the intent of offering it up to God, and so he too is not bound by karma. Not only that -- through the Name of God the devotee becomes entirely free of karma (nishkarma).

_Deh dhare nishkarmapanu nathi, pan naa mahelu Hari naam, paamesh naam sharan vade, nishkarmapanu nirvan. ||8||_ (Even though souls take on bodies in order to be free of the bondage of karma, freedom from karma is not thereby attained. But the devotee says: I shall never give up the Name of God; therefore I am certain that through refuge in the Name of God I shall in the end attain the state free of karma.)

He further says, in the Vadughol, verse 7:

_Karma tano bhay tahan lagi huto e, Hari Hari jahan lagi tuj thaki veg loe, prakruti narke jeev sanchariyo, Hari Hari bhatiyo narkani kodand kod._ (For as long as the soul stayed apart from devotion to God, for that long alone did it fear the bondage of karma. For, from the moment the soul entered into material nature -- prakriti-maya -- it has been buried in hell crore upon crore of times.)

_Karma bandhan chhediyan, sanjhori chare khan, antak maarag lopiyo, Hindola re Parbrahm bhakt paran, Hindola re yog adhyatam saar. ||7||_ (He cut away the bonds of karma, and out of the four wombs He fashioned a rattle to shake for God, who lies cradled in the swing; thus He erased the path to Yama's abode. In such a cradle-swing, Parbrahm holds His devotee dear, and keeps love for him.)

_Gyan vairag toran karya, ane sthambh Shankar Brahma, nishkarma bhakti hindoldo, Hindola re hinche hinche Hari Parbrahm. ||8||_ (He made a cradle of knowledge and dispassion, with Shankar and Brahma as its posts. Such a cradle-swing is made of karma-free devotion, and in that swing God Parbrahm swings and rocks.)

Adhyaruji, giving counsel, says:

_Karam vishwanu talva, ane galva gun beej, sansar paar utarva, jaachne Jugdish. ||4||_ (In order to overcome the karma of the whole world, and to bury -- that is, destroy -- the seed of the three gunas, and to be delivered from the ocean of worldly existence, make your plea to God devotedly.)

Umavlo means an eager surging, an overflowing, a foaming rush of enthusiasm -- a state in which repeated upsurges keep occurring. In such a state, sometimes false upsurges of maya arise, and the soul makes a mistake and gets swept off onto the wrong path. Speaking of this in the Umavalo, Adhyaruji says:

_Padhiyo padhiyo re lahyo chare Ved e, karam marag re bhulyo bhamyo e, na janiyo re lahyo bhaktino bhed e, hun anek ranto sir aani e._ (Having studied the four Vedas, the soul went astray on the path of ritual karma and kept wandering in the bonds of karma, because it did not grasp the secret of the path of devotion to God; and so it kept holding in its mind attachments of many kinds, such as "I" and "mine." Therefore, O yellow-robed Parbrahm Padmanabhji, my God, I have come to the refuge of Your feet.)

Practice devotion with such eager fervor for remembering His Name. Regarding souls in the cage of karma, Maharaj Jivanji says in the Samagam:

_Ek alla (matika) the do bhaya, ko ghoda ko mir, aato saato Jivna, nar samajhat nahi bepir. ||149||_ (Out of the same clay -- the five great elements -- God fashioned souls of two kinds of nature. Among them He made some like horses, laboring to enjoy sense-pleasures, and He made others victors who gained mastery over sensual desire.)

But he who enjoys the pleasures of sensual desire in this way can only enjoy those pleasures if, like a horse, he bears the burden of the world; whereas those who do not care for sensory pleasures can become like victorious generals who enjoy supreme happiness and peace. Thus, in place of laboring to enjoy sense-pleasures, one may instead enjoy such pleasures directly, and if one does not care for sense-objects, one may enjoy supreme happiness -- in this way, such enjoyment comes about through an exchange of labor. Foolish people such as these do not understand this.

**Entry into the Cage of Karma -- Its Release: Guru and Sadguru Are One**

Third Question -- Jivandasji said to Haribhai: In creating this creation, He made a cage for the soul. With the five elements and three gunas -- these eight aspects -- the soul entered into the cage. And again the Merciful Lord said: "Soul, enter this cage." Then the soul awoke and said: "Maharaj, You are sending me into this entry of karma-yoga -- then by what means shall I now attain You?" When it said this, the Merciful Lord said: "Brother, count the food and movement of the senses as little; enjoy your wife but once; and take subtle food, not much more than one ser -- five hundred grams -- of grain; and thereby conquer the eleven senses (the five senses of knowledge and the five organs of action)." -- A sakhi (couplet) follows:

_Kabir tanki bhukh alpa hai, teen paanv ke sher, manki bhukh agaadh hai, gal jaay Mer Sumer. ||1||_ (Das Kabirji says: the hunger of the body is of only a very small measure -- it is satisfied by three-quarters of a ser, about 375 grams, or a full ser of about 500 grams, of food. But the hunger of the mind is exceedingly deep; in it, even great mountains like Meru and Sumeru could sink, so vast is its depth.)

For this the Merciful Lord said: "Consider the five elements and three gunas as dwelling with Me; you will not thereby fail to become My devotee. Wherever you stay and remember Me, there I am present before you. By your own good will, even in the stationary and moving beings, in insects and birds, I shall not let you keep any attached share in the three gunas and five elements -- that is, hold no attachment there. This is My true word." Thus, at that gathering of creation, the Merciful Lord gave His word to the soul.

In your tradition, in the seventh verse (aad) of the fourth kadvu of Adhyaruji, the word is spoken:

_Have rakho re have rakho re, Swami aapan mahen, aapno vol sambharajo._ (O Master, now keep this soul in Your refuge. Keep it in Your refuge -- for You Yourself have said:)

_sarva-dharman parityajya mam ekam sharanam vraja, aham tva sarva-papebhyo mokshayishyami ma shuchah. ||66||_ (Abandoning all duties, come to Me alone for refuge; I shall release you from all sins -- do not grieve.)

For that reason, when this attention is lost, great greed befalls the soul as well. The Merciful Lord has said, "Wherever you dwell and worship, there I am" -- yet it is the soul itself that keeps holding on to its own attached share; not taking heed of this, it must wander in the round of birth and rebirth. If it understands, its wandering ceases, and it attains contentment and merges into the form of God. "Knowing Me to dwell in the stationary and moving," He says, "consider well your original share in the eight aspects." The three gunas and five elements that the Merciful Lord has spoken of -- forgetting these and disregarding them, the soul, having forgotten the form of God, still goes about seeing Vasudevji in the stationary and moving world, yet still does not understand. And so it has drifted from birth to birth. In this way it has, of its own doing, led its own soul astray. For this reason no soul attains God. On this, the word from the fifth verse (aad) of the first kadvu of Adhyaruji:

_Sacharachar jene bholvyu, bholvyu vividh vichar, prakruti tane gune vahiyo, mohiyo bhame re sansar._ (The one who has deluded all stationary and moving beings -- He has deluded them with manifold thoughts. Carried along by the strands of nature, the deluded soul wanders in the world.)

All beings in the world, stationary and moving, have been deluded through the foundation of the three gunas, deluded into all sorts of separate thoughts and intentions. In this way, subjugated to the qualities of maya, they keep wandering in the wheel of this world amid so many kinds of thoughts and counter-thoughts.

For this, the Vaishnav Jivandasji said to Haribhai that the soul, by becoming subject to material nature-maya, has erred in discernment; but Vasudevji has not deluded it. That day, in that same way, under the mahuda tree, the question-and-answer session, with its illustrations and occasions, was thus completed.

The Vaishnav Jivandasji further said: the soul is void -- caught in the noose of infatuation with material nature, its heart made empty, cut off from its own true duty, without a guru. Without a guru, how can one's inborn tendencies and the disorders of the senses be given up? And without a sadguru, who will carry one across? Jivandasji said: the soul that does not attain God is the one that, by its own doing, keeps treating guru and sadguru as two separate things; but on the day these two come together as one, it attains God. There is an illustration for this. The soul, having gone round through the eighty-four lakh species, has come to stand in a human body. It stands at the court that is the heart, at the door of the Lord, and lodges its complaint. What the first guru tells it is called the "complaint" -- but as long as the Master has not heard and granted redress, the matter remains unresolved. When that Master hears the plea and comes forward eagerly to meet it, then the sadguru is found -- that is called "redress heard."

For this, the word of the [first] verse of the first kadvu:

_Hari Hari samarath Parbrahm anusaryo e, bhagyo ati sandeh, bhay saghala have nirdalya e._ (Ah! When I began to practice devotion to the all-powerful Parbrahm and to live accordingly, my great doubt of falling life after life vanished, and every fear of the bondage of karma fled and was destroyed.)

This same sentiment also appears in a verse from the aarti kirtan:

_Bhale aaviya Parbrahm Ram, samarath dhanine sante seviya e._ (O Padmanabhji, form of Parbrahm, it is very good that You have come. Saints such as You are all-powerful, and so they release the disciple from the bonds of the karma of many lifetimes.)

Maharaj Jivanji says:

_Likhya mite nahi Jivna, je kachhu likhiya lekh, sad-sadguru lekh mitaiya, tab paaya aap alekh. ||39||_ (Maharaj Jivandasji says: whatever record of karma the Ordainer has written cannot be erased even by more karma; but the Sadguru has erased such a written record of karmic bondage -- and then, O Lord, we were able to attain You, whom otherwise none could come to know.)

_likhita chitraguptena lalatakshar-malika, tan na chalayitum shakya asuraih tri-dashaur api._ (It is said elsewhere in the Puranas: the garland of letters that Chitragupta has written on the forehead -- neither the gods nor the demons have the power to move it.)

_yad yatra likhitam bhale tan nrishtham naiva jayate, rite Shri Ramdasanam prem nirbhar chetasam._ (Whatever the Ordainer has written on the forehead never becomes false -- except that this rule applies to all others, but not to Ramdas devotees whose hearts are full of supreme love.)

For this, the word of Kabir's kahera (couplet-refrain) has been quoted in the Samagam, and its refrain-verse (abhog) has been written down there. Here we shall look at the whole of that pada (hymn). The sentiments contained in this pada are very much worth understanding. In Handwritten Manuscript no. 8, page 125, the raga of this pada is given as Godi, but it can also be set to the raga Bilaval.

**(Raga Godi)**

_Rehta mera jarjara, kaantu jhina soot re. (Tek)
Jal jaai thal upni re, aai nagar aap.
Ek achamba mein suna, betdiye jaaya baap. ||1||
Bava mera byah karo, koou tumsa var laayo.
Jab lagi var paaun nahi, baba tab lagi tumhi bihayo. ||2||
Ek badiya jin karo, dooja mari mari jaao.
Jine mera raihera dhada, main to taahike sang rahaao. ||3||
Kahat Kabir sohi nar gyata (jaaga), is padka kare vichar.
Pahele parche guru kiya, sadguru le utare paar. ||4||_

In a hidden, profound sense Das Kabirji says: this frail, worn-out spinning-wheel of mine is this body; with it I spin a very fine, delicate thread -- that is, through this body I spin, as it were, the fine thread of knowledge and wisdom, my fancies and imaginings. This body, born from the water that is a drop, has appeared in the form of an earthly body, come forth into this city that is the world. I have heard one truly astonishing thing: a daughter has given birth to her father! This is a matter of surat-nirat (inward attention and absorption). When absorption (tallinata) comes, that is the "daughter"; and once absorption has come, the vision of God (bhagavad-darshan) occurs -- so it is only the daughter that is fine thread and absorption who can make manifest the Supreme Father as "Father." That is, only once a son or daughter is born can a man be called that child's father; before the birth of the son, no one can be called "father." So it is a wonder indeed that the son has given birth to the father. O elder, now arrange my marriage -- to such a bridegroom as is as powerful as You. Until I attain such a husband, keep me betrothed to You alone. Do one thing so great: never give me such a husband that, should one die, the next would die too. Rather, I shall stay only with that Creator who has fashioned this body of mine, wheel-spun through the eighty-four lakh births. Kabirji says: that man alone will be truly awake and wise who is able to reflect on the deep meaning of the words given in this pada. Such a person will have taken as guru the one who, through a first acquaintance, gives him understanding; and through a second, deeper acquaintance, the sadguru will carry him across the ocean of worldly existence.

A pada related to this one appears in Kabirvani, Year 10, Issue 114, page 1. This pada is also found in Najar Note no. 13, page 177; its explanation has been presented very beautifully in Kabirvani -- let us look at it.

**(Raga Sorath)**

_Mere piyu to base re agampuri, milna kaise hoy? (Tek)
Haanji dhundhat dhundhat jarjarya, khevat mat baal.
Dhundha mara jajara.
Virah rupi (behal) nadiya vahe, kis bidh utaru paar? ||1||
Haanji patiya likh likh bhejti, koi na kahe re sandesh.
Jis nagarimein Halam base, kaun kahe re sandesh. ||2||
Paap punya dou vaniya, vishaya lagi re (rachyo re) bajar.
Ketke soda kar gayo, ketek aavanhaar. ||3||
Kahe Kabir suno sadhuva, sab mili karo re vichar.
Pahelo parche guru mile, dooje sarajanhaar. ||4||_

Das Kabirji says: my Husband dwells in a hidden city beyond comprehension -- how, then, can I meet Him? Ah, searching for Him, my very body has grown worn and frail; and my ferryman, that is, my guru, is utterly blissful. The river that makes for such a wretched state -- the river of separation -- flows on; how then shall I cross to the far shore? Ah, I write letters and send them, but no one brings back word. In which city my beloved Husband dwells, what country that is -- no one tells me; no one gives any message about it, no one brings word. Sin and merit are two merchants who have set up the marketplace of sensory desire, and some have already done their trading in it, while still others' trade in karma is yet to come. Das Kabirji says: O saints and sadhus, listen -- gather together and reflect on this matter, that with this my Husband, at the first meeting I found the guru, and at the second encounter I found the Creator-Lord.

[Glossary:] khevat (boatman) = guru; patiyan = letters; vaniya = merchant; ketke = some. A detailed exposition of the above pada has been given in Kabir Vani, Year 10, Issue 114, from page 1 onward, as follows: This pada is extremely well known among us.

In the scriptures, devotion (bhakti) is recognized as being of two kinds: primary (mukhya) devotion and secondary (gauna) devotion. Primary devotion is the devotion practiced by forming a bond of love with God; in it, there is only the longing for the vision (darshan) of the Lord. In secondary devotion, on the other hand, desires of many kinds are mixed in; sometimes God is even set aside altogether. Even without acquaintance with God, and without love for Him, devotion is practiced by adopting some fixed ritual procedure in order to fulfill some desire of the mind; such devotion is therefore also called vaidhi (ritual, rule-bound) devotion. Thus, in secondary or vaidhi devotion, importance is given to some desire or procedure other than God Himself; whereas in primary devotion, nothing other than God is even considered -- only love and passionate attachment (raag) toward God alone arise. The saints therefore call it ragatmika bhakti, devotion born of passionate love. In this pada we see ragatmika bhakti, or primary devotion. God is regarded as the Beloved, and the soul as His beloved lady. The beloved lady remains absorbed in the sweet remembrance of her Beloved. The soul has an intensely fervent longing for the vision of God; yet the possibility of that vision does not appear to be forming, because the soul is in ignorance. It has no acquaintance with the abode of God, nor any knowledge of the path to reach it; yet, all the while, its longing for that vision grows more and more intense -- and it is this very state of the soul that is described at the very opening of this pada.

In such a state, the soul looks for help. It hopes that some assistance might come. It becomes convinced that only if it meets someone who truly knows the secret can it reach its destination. But no such knower is met with. Without a boatman-guru, or such a knower of the secret, it seems extremely hard for the soul to cross the river of separation flowing in between; still, it keeps trying by every means to obtain help. Whoever offers help offers it, but only superficially, because God remains beyond reach -- the soul has neither experienced God nor beheld His abode. All it knows is that the abode of God is called Agampuri (the unreachable city). And so the soul, seeking God, wanders here and there without rest. If someone says He will be found in the Himalayas, it runs off to the Himalayas. If someone says He will be found at a place of pilgrimage, it goes on pilgrimage after pilgrimage. If someone says He will be found in a temple, it goes to temples and performs every ritual there too. Yet no one can satisfy its hunger for the vision of God. If, in this moment of longing, the soul finds no help, its state becomes like that of a spring drying up in the desert.

Therefore, in the closing lines, Kabir Saheb, instructing the sadhus, puts this message before the world. An appeal is made to the sadhus to gather together and deliberate; but that sadhus are unable to gather together is the greatest tragedy of all. Envy, malice, and enmity are all to be found among sadhus. Sadhus have not been able to free themselves from the very faults of ordinary people; hence the question arises -- whom should one call a sadhu? Should one who preaches religion and morality in public while practicing unrighteousness in private be called a sadhu? Or should one who merely dons saffron robes and renounces the world be called a sadhu? Should one with long hair and beard, smeared with ash, begging for alms, be called a sadhu? Kabir Saheb says to the sadhus: gather together and deliberate -- the true sadhu is the one who labors to move from untruth toward truth, or who is ever moving from darkness toward light. Not only that, but the garb of a sadhu can rightly be worn only by one who continually holds good thoughts, forms good resolves, behaves well, and inspires others toward good as well. Such sadhus are true sadhus, and only such sadhus, gathering together, can truly deliberate and can lead the world onto the path of well-being.

But today there is a dearth of people capable of guiding society. Who today, breaking free from the center of self-interest, can think of others? The condition that existed six hundred years ago is the very same condition that exists in the present age. Sadhus become "sants" and then become masters of a gaddi (a seat of religious authority). A web of scheming keeps being woven. Like any householder, such a person too remains absorbed in preserving his gaddi. As a result, though living within society, he remains distant from it. To preserve a gaddi one needs a following; to gather a following one needs wealth; and to gather wealth one must deceive society. In this way, the welfare of society cannot come about through such a corrupt path. Instead, he fills a marketplace of sense-objects and lures people. When collecting donations, he says, "We will have your name engraved on a marble plaque." A man's ego is thereby fed; the desire for honor and fame is stoked. As a result, even a competition in giving donations gets arranged -- people take part in it so that their own fame may increase. Meanwhile, in this flowing river of donations, the gaddi-masters enjoy their own pleasures and live in comfort and indulgence. Such a vicious cycle keeps turning; from time immemorial, people have come and gone, been born and died. In that marketplace of sense-objects, each departs after having struck his bargains. What does he carry away with him? Only the impressions (vasanas) of sin and merit. Since the days of Baba Adam, the soul has kept its journey going, carrying along a store of greed and infatuation.

This is exactly the point to reflect on. All have come in darkness -- come with their eyes shut. And when they go, they too go in darkness with their eyes shut. Where did they come from? Where have they ended up? Who sent them? Who kept them alive while they were in the mother's womb? Who filled the mother's womb with nourishment? Such questions never even arise in the soul. When such questions do arise, know that one's good fortune has dawned; only when the grace of God comes about do such questions awaken in the mind -- and from the very moment such questions awaken, that soul's journey toward the good (shreya-yatra) is reckoned to have begun. Within its inner being, a wind of transformation begins to blow; little by little, the tamasic forces diminish, and the inner self grows steady in a sattvic disposition. Bad qualities fall away, and a continuous process of purification goes on. Such progress is what we call the shreya-yatra, the journey toward the good.

Before the journey toward the good begins, the experience of a love-triangle inevitably occurs. The soul wishes to form a bond of love with God, but before its wish can be carried out, it enters into a relationship with maya. A close, entangled dealing with maya begins. Maya keeps manifesting before the soul in the form of objects and sense-pleasures. The soul truly comes to revel in the enchantments of the world. At that time, the soul does not even remember God, because maya's colorful, decorated, enchanting form, full of objects and sense-pleasures, never departs from its mind.

Once this special, distinctive attraction of maya has taken hold, talk of God begins to seem like idle chatter to the soul. Thoughts of God feel pointless. Those who speak of Him, those who preach Him, come to seem like bitter poison. Yes, sometimes a flash of lightning does occur -- that is true -- but only when calamity strikes. Then the soul makes do with a makeshift lamp and wick: it sings a bhajan or two, gets into the habit of visiting temples, and observes a vow or two. But as time passes, these too are forgotten, one after another, and by whatever reckoning, the soul settles into a merely mental sort of contentment. Even if a flash of God's grace has occurred, the soul is unable to make use of it. Once again, in the marketplace of sense-objects, the soul goes on striking ever new bargains in fresh acts of karma.

This whole saga of the love-triangle needs to be reflected upon carefully. What is the nature of maya? Where does maya reside? The scriptures and the saints say that maya belongs to God Himself. It is especially necessary to recognize the relationship between maya and Maya's Lord, God. If we form a bond of love with the Lord of Maya, then maya no longer torments the soul; rather, it tries to become favorable to the soul on its journey toward the good. Maya then becomes a maidservant and turns into a help.

Some call material nature (prakriti) maya; some call ignorance (avidya) maya. Maya exists in many different forms; yet its true dwelling place is in the mind alone. In the form of desire, in the form of craving, in the form of thirst, it keeps arising in the mind like bubbles. Whatever object comes before one's eyes, that object begins to be liked. Liking and disliking are the manifest form of maya. Once an object is liked, the wish to obtain it arises, and one tries, by whatever means, to obtain it. In this way, the wheel of maya keeps turning. Infatuation and possessiveness are maya's companions; the attraction toward them keeps forever growing. As a result, the soul forgets God and becomes engrossed in striking bargains over sense-objects in maya's marketplace.

Therefore it is beneficial that those in society who call themselves sadhus should first fully grasp the reality of this love-triangle, because becoming a gaddi-master is itself to be reckoned as falling into maya. How can one who remains sunk in maya remember Maya's Lord? So it is well if one tries to keep apart from maya. As for the idea of withdrawing from the world altogether, that is of no use -- every soul will have to take birth into this world, and so there is no benefit in disregarding the world. The soul must indeed come into the world; it will just as surely have to resolve to live rightly. When hungry, one must eat; when thirsty, one must drink water. Whatever is necessary for the nourishment of this body must indeed be done, and one must act according to one's destiny (prarabdha). Even so, what is wrong in that?

Once born, one will naturally have relationships with mother, father, brothers, and sisters; once one becomes a householder, one will naturally have sons and daughters too. Mother, father, brothers, sisters, sons, and daughters are, in themselves, not any form of maya at all -- it is the desire and craving one holds for these people that is maya. Since the form of maya is, in this way, born of craving, it is from that standpoint that such cravings ought to be uprooted from the mind. Just as a boat floats on water, so one must learn to float across the ocean of worldly existence. If water fills the boat, the boat sinks and can never float again; likewise, if worldly cravings begin to fill the mind, one sinks into the ocean of worldly existence. If one wishes to cross the ocean of birth and death (bhavsagar), it is necessary to root out worldly attachments from the mind -- and that alone is what is meant by "becoming separate from maya."

That husband and wife should love each other can be understood; but if that love is born of infatuation, it drowns one. One ought really to reflect on whether a husband's love for his wife is for her body, or for the consciousness dwelling within that body. If the love were for the body, then after she dies he ought not to take her to the cremation ground; yet, in fact, the body must be taken to the cremation ground, for otherwise it begins to stink and to rot. From this it is necessary to understand that it is the conscious principle (chetan tattva) alone that the soul holds most dear; even after death that consciousness continues to be remembered. Therefore the soul ought to form a bond of love with that consciousness and become steadfast in it. Only if sadhus themselves cultivate this kind of understanding can they explain it to others in society.

The soul in whom sudden love toward God awakens -- to that soul, God certainly sends help in one form or another. When such a soul becomes utterly overwhelmed with feeling for God, God Himself sends a guru to meet it. Without the grace of God, one does not attain the vision (darshan) of a guru. In our own land there lived Paramahansa Yoganandji. On his guru's instruction, he went to America and propagated the science of yoga there. From 1920 to 1952 CE he carried out the finest possible propagation of Indian culture in America. Even today, the ashrams he established are still there and continue to direct yoga-related activities across the whole world. One wonderful episode from his life comes to mind here.

He was studying in Calcutta at the time, a student in college. His boundless love for God had grown so great that he made many efforts to find a guru. In those days, in Calcutta, the name of Master Mahashay was well known -- Master Mahashay was a disciple of Shri Ramakrishna Paramahansa. Yoganandji felt drawn to him and would meet him again and again. One day, intending to install him as his guru, he made a garland of flowers and went to him. Before he could even say a word about his own feelings, Master Mahashay already knew what was in Yoganandji's heart. After Yoganandji had paid his respects and was about to place the garland upon him, Master Mahashay stopped him, saying: "I am not your guru. Your guru will meet you very soon." Some time then passed. Yoganandji kept feeling an eager longing for his true guru to appear. He went from Calcutta to Banaras for his studies; there too he continued longing for his guru --
